CEFR levels are estimates written for this project. The CEFR describes what a learner can do, not which grammar to learn, so no official grammar list exists for it. The official CEFR global scale (Council of Europe, Common European Framework of Reference for Languages, 2001), first sentence of each level: A1 "Can understand and use familiar everyday expressions and very basic phrases aimed at the satisfaction of needs of a concrete type." A2 "Can understand sentences and frequently used expressions related to areas of most immediate relevance (e.g. very basic personal and family information, shopping, local geography, employment)." B1 "Can understand the main points of clear standard input on familiar matters regularly encountered in work, school, leisure, etc." B2 "Can understand the main ideas of complex text on both concrete and abstract topics, including technical discussions in his/her field of specialisation." C1 "Can understand a wide range of demanding, longer texts, and recognise implicit meaning." C2 "Can understand with ease virtually everything heard or read." The copyright of the scales belongs to the Council of Europe; these are short quotations.

Each lesson's summary and each planned point's title ends with its estimated CEFR level; a range (A2–B1) means it's commonly taught at either. The level band is the earliest one: A1 absolute-beginner or beginner, A2 beginner-intermediate, B1 intermediate, B2 advanced-intermediate, C1 and C2 advanced.
title: German first grammar
intro: German puts the verb in a fixed place, and it marks gender on the article rather than on the noun's ending alone. These lessons cover sein, the present tense, der/die/das, verb-second word order, the accusative, and nicht versus kein. Nouns are written with a capital letter. The CEFR level after each point (A1 to C2) is an estimate, and a range like A2–B1 means it often comes up at both.

lessons.title: sein — “to be”
lessons.summary: bin, bist, ist, and the plural. (about A1)

sections.p: sein is irregular, and you learn it first because almost every introduction uses it. ich bin “I am”, du bist “you are” (one person you know), er ist / sie ist / es ist “he / she / it is”.
wir sind “we are”, ihr seid “you are” (several people you know), sie sind “they are”. The polite “you”, to a stranger, is Sie sind — the same form as “they”, but written with a capital S.

drills.why: To one person you know: du bist.
Polite Sie takes sind, and the verb comes first in a yes/no question.

lessons.title: The present tense
lessons.summary: Regular endings on a verb like machen. (about A1)

sections.p: Most verbs add an ending to the stem (machen → mach-). ich mache, du machst, er macht, wir machen, ihr macht, sie machen. The polite Sie uses the wir form: Sie machen.
German has one present. ich lerne is both “I learn” and “I am learning”.

drills.why: er/sie/es takes -t, and arbeiten keeps the e: arbeitet.
The present covers “I learn” and “I am learning”.

lessons.title: der, die, das
lessons.summary: Three genders, and the indefinite article. (about A1)

sections.p: Every noun is masculine, feminine or neuter, and the article shows it. Nominative (the subject): der Mann, die Frau, das Kind. Plural subjects take die whatever the gender: die Kinder. Nouns are capitalized.
“A” is ein with masculine and neuter, eine with feminine. German often leaves “a” out with professions: sie ist Ärztin “she is a doctor”.

lessons.title: The verb in second place
lessons.summary: Statements keep the verb second; yes/no questions put it first. (about A1)

sections.p: In a statement the conjugated verb is the second idea, not necessarily the second word. Ich lerne heute Deutsch and Heute lerne ich Deutsch are both fine. If something else starts the sentence, the subject slips in after the verb.
A yes/no question starts with the verb: Lernst du Deutsch? Question words stay first, and the verb is still second: Wo wohnst du?

drills.why: Heute takes the first slot, so the verb comes next and ich follows it.
A yes/no question starts with the verb.
Wo is first; the verb is second.
Subject, then the verb, then the rest.
Morgen is first; wir fahren keeps the verb second.

lessons.title: The accusative
lessons.summary: The direct object, and the one article that changes. (about A1)

sections.p: The direct object is in the accusative. Feminine die and neuter das look the same as the subject. Masculine der becomes den, and ein becomes einen.
Word order is free enough that the article, not the position, tells you the job. Den Mann sieht die Frau still means the woman sees the man, because den is the object.

drills.q: Den Mann sieht die Frau. Who sees whom?
drills.why: den Mann is the object; die Frau is the subject.

lessons.title: nicht and kein
lessons.summary: Saying no to a verb, and “no” plus a noun. (about A1)

sections.p: nicht negates the verb or the whole sentence, and it usually sits late: Ich trinke nicht “I don't drink”, Ich lerne heute nicht.
kein means “not a / no” and replaces ein. It takes the same endings: kein Kaffee, keine Milch, keinen Apfel (masculine object).

drills.en: I don't have any coffee. (masculine object)
drills.why: kein replaces ein, and the masculine object takes -en.
An adjective is negated with nicht.
